difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain in a pharmacology context. The correct answer addresses a non-obvious intermediate link (bioavailability vs. dosage). Trap choices either strengthen a neighboring premise or introduce plausible but irrelevant comparisons.
stimulus: A clinical trial found that patients who took a new anti-inflammatory drug experienced significantly reduced joint swelling within two weeks. Because the drug inhibits the enzyme COX-2, researchers concluded that COX-2 inhibition is the mechanism responsible for the reduction in joint swelling observed in the trial participants.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients in the trial who reported taking the drug consistently showed measurably higher blood plasma concentrations of the drug than did patients who reported occasional missed doses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several other drugs that also inhibit COX-2 have independently been shown to reduce joint swelling in patients with the same inflammatory condition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The trial excluded patients who were simultaneously taking any other anti-inflammatory medication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: COX-2 is present in elevated concentrations in the joint tissue of patients suffering from the type of inflammation the drug was designed to treat.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some patients in the trial experienced mild gastrointestinal side effects, which are commonly associated with COX-2 inhibitors.

explanations.correct: If multiple independent drugs that share only the COX-2-inhibiting mechanism all reduce joint swelling, this strongly corroborates that COX-2 inhibition is the mechanism at work—not some other property unique to this particular drug. This directly supports the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Strengthens a premise about drug compliance and dosage, not the conclusion that COX-2 inhibition is the mechanism. This is the 'strengthens a neighboring claim' trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Independent replication across different COX-2 inhibitors confirms the mechanism link, ruling out drug-specific properties as the true cause.
explanations.C: Rules out a confound (co-medication), which supports the internal validity of the trial, but does not specifically support COX-2 inhibition as the mechanism over other properties of this drug.
explanations.D: Shows COX-2 is present at the site of inflammation—a plausible-sounding anatomical fact—but does not show that inhibiting COX-2 causes the reduction in swelling. This is an 'accurate but irrelevant' trap.
explanations.E: The side-effect profile is consistent with COX-2 activity but does not address whether COX-2 inhibition causes the therapeutic effect. This is an unwarranted comparison trap.

difficultyReason: EXCEPT format reverses the task. The argument involves a policy chain about environmental regulation. Four choices each support a link in the chain; students under time pressure select the first strengthener they find rather than identifying the one that does not strengthen.
stimulus: Economist: Placing a cap-and-trade limit on industrial carbon emissions will reduce the total volume of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere. When the total volume of atmospheric carbon dioxide declines, average global temperatures will stabilize. Therefore, cap-and-trade policies should be enacted if governments are serious about preventing further climate disruption.
questionStem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the economist's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historical data show that periods of lower industrial carbon emissions correlate with slower rates of atmospheric carbon dioxide accumulation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Industries subject to cap-and-trade regimes in pilot regions have consistently reduced their total carbon emissions to comply with the caps.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atmospheric scientists have demonstrated that stabilizing carbon dioxide levels halts the primary feedback mechanism driving global temperature increases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cap-and-trade systems have generated substantial government revenue that some nations have reinvested in renewable energy infrastructure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Countries that have enacted cap-and-trade policies report higher rates of industrial investment in low-carbon technologies than countries that have not.

explanations.correct: D describes a revenue benefit of cap-and-trade systems—a separate advantage that does not bear on whether the policy reduces atmospheric carbon dioxide or stabilizes temperatures. It neither closes a logical gap in the argument nor rules out an alternative. It does not strengthen the economist's specific causal chain.
explanations.A: Strengthens—confirms the premise that reduced industrial emissions lower atmospheric CO₂ accumulation.
explanations.B: Strengthens—confirms that cap-and-trade actually succeeds in reducing industrial emissions, supporting the first causal link.
explanations.C: Strengthens—confirms the second causal link that stabilizing CO₂ stabilizes temperatures.
explanations.D: Correct (does not strengthen). Revenue reinvestment is a collateral benefit, not part of the argument's causal chain.
explanations.E: Strengthens—suggests cap-and-trade promotes structural change that sustains lower emissions over time.

difficultyReason: Analogical argument across legal jurisdictions. Correct answer closes the analogical gap. Distractors include one that strengthens a neighboring claim about recidivism generally and one that reverses causal direction.
stimulus: Advocates for juvenile justice reform in State X point out that State Y reduced its juvenile recidivism rate by 35 percent after replacing mandatory minimum sentences for juvenile offenders with individualized rehabilitation programs. They argue that State X would achieve a comparable reduction in juvenile recidivism if it adopted the same reform.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the advocates' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juvenile recidivism in State X is currently higher than it was in State Y before State Y enacted its reform.

choices.label: B
choices.text: State X's juvenile offender population has a demographic and offense-type profile closely similar to that of State Y's juvenile offender population prior to State Y's reform.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rehabilitation programs generally produce better long-term behavioral outcomes than punitive sentences for adult offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: State Y's juvenile recidivism rate has continued to decline in the years following the initial 35 percent reduction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several advocacy organizations in State X have publicly endorsed individualized rehabilitation as the preferred approach for juvenile offenders.

explanations.correct: The analogical argument depends on State X being sufficiently similar to State Y for the same intervention to produce the same result. Confirming that their juvenile offender populations are closely similar in demographic and offense-type profile closes the most critical gap in the analogy.
explanations.A: Higher baseline recidivism in State X could suggest more room for improvement, but it does not confirm that the same intervention would work—it could equally mean State X's problem is structurally different. This is the 'accurate but potentially irrelevant' trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Similarity of populations is the load-bearing assumption of any analogical policy argument.
explanations.C: Strengthens a general claim about rehabilitation vs. punishment for adults, not the specific analogy about juvenile programs in two comparable states. This is the 'strengthens a different conclusion' trap.
explanations.D: Shows continued improvement in State Y but says nothing about whether the same would hold in State X. This is the 'unwarranted comparison' trap.
explanations.E: Endorsement by advocacy organizations is irrelevant to whether the policy would actually achieve the reduction. This is the 'accurate but irrelevant' trap.

difficultyReason: Multi-step causal argument in linguistics. The correct answer confirms a non-obvious intermediate mechanism (phonological salience vs. frequency). Trap choices include one that introduces an alternative explanation disguised as support.
stimulus: Linguists studying the acquisition of vocabulary in bilingual children noted that children in the study learned cognate words—words that share similar sounds and meanings across two languages—significantly faster than non-cognate words. The linguists concluded that phonological similarity between languages accelerates vocabulary acquisition in bilingual children.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cognate words used in the study appeared with roughly equal frequency in the bilingual children's daily exposure to both languages as the non-cognate words used in the study.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bilingual children generally outperform monolingual children on standardized vocabulary tests by the time they reach school age.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bilingual children in the study were drawn from households where both languages were spoken with approximately equal regularity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some non-cognate words that were semantically simple were learned as quickly as certain cognate words in the study.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Among the children in the study, those who received explicit instruction in phonological patterns learned cognate words at a faster rate than those who did not.

explanations.correct: The most obvious alternative explanation for why cognates were learned faster is that cognates simply appear more frequently in children's input. Ruling out this frequency confound—by showing cognate and non-cognate words appeared equally often—directly supports the conclusion that phonological similarity, not exposure frequency, is responsible.
explanations.A: Correct. This rules out input frequency as an alternative explanation, supporting the phonological similarity mechanism.
explanations.B: A general claim about bilingual advantage—strengthens a different, broader conclusion about bilingualism, not the specific mechanism identified. This is the 'strengthens a different conclusion' trap.
explanations.C: Equal household exposure rules out a language-dominance confound, which is a mild strengthener for the study's internal validity but does not address the key mechanistic claim about phonological similarity. Weaker than (A) and primarily supports a premise rather than the conclusion.
explanations.D: The existence of exceptions to the cognate-advantage pattern weakens the conclusion rather than strengthening it. This is the 'opposite answer' trap.
explanations.E: Shows that explicit instruction in phonological patterns amplifies the cognate advantage—which could suggest instruction, not natural phonological similarity, is the operative variable. This is a disguised alternative-cause trap.

difficultyReason: Policy argument about technology and labor economics. Correct answer addresses an implicit load-bearing assumption about substitutability. Trap choices include one that is topically relevant but strengthens a collateral premise and one that is a subtle weakener.
stimulus: A think tank argues that widespread adoption of automated warehouse management systems will reduce employment among warehouse workers in the logistics sector. The think tank notes that in the three distribution centers that have already adopted these systems, the number of full-time warehouse positions has declined by an average of 40 percent within eighteen months of implementation.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the think tank's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The three distribution centers that adopted automated systems also expanded their storage capacity significantly during the same eighteen-month period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Logistics companies that have not yet adopted automated systems are planning to do so within the next five years in order to remain competitive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Workers displaced from the three distribution centers were not subsequently rehired in other roles within the same logistics companies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tasks performed by automated warehouse management systems are virtually identical to those previously performed by the full-time warehouse workers who lost their positions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Automated warehouse management systems require periodic technical maintenance performed by specialized engineers who are not drawn from the existing warehouse workforce.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes that automation substitutes for human labor rather than merely augmenting it or filling new roles. Confirming that the automated systems perform tasks virtually identical to those the displaced workers performed directly supports the substitution claim and bolsters the conclusion that automation reduces employment.
explanations.A: If capacity expanded, one would expect more workers to be needed—the 40% decline despite expansion actually makes the automation effect look stronger, but this choice introduces a confound that could raise questions. However, this describes conditions at the study sites without directly confirming the substitution mechanism. Less targeted than (D).
explanations.B: Shows the phenomenon is likely to spread widely, which supports the breadth of the prediction but does not confirm the mechanism that automation actually causes the employment reduction. This is the 'accurate but strengthens a different aspect' trap.
explanations.C: Rules out the possibility that displaced workers were absorbed elsewhere in the same companies—this supports the argument somewhat, but only addresses a narrow reabsorption alternative rather than the core mechanism. Weaker than (D).
explanations.D: Correct. Task substitutability is the load-bearing assumption; confirming it directly closes the mechanistic gap.
explanations.E: Introduces a new type of job (maintenance engineers) that is not drawn from the warehouse workforce—this actually suggests automation creates jobs that are inaccessible to displaced workers, which is more of a collateral detail than a strengthener of the core causal claim. Could be read as weakening (workers can't move into the new roles) or neutral.

difficultyReason: Historical causation argument. The correct answer rules out a sophisticated alternative explanation (confounding historical variable). Multiple trap choices are topically resonant and appear to support the argument without actually addressing the core causal inference.
stimulus: Historians have argued that the dramatic increase in agricultural productivity in medieval Europe between the tenth and twelfth centuries was caused primarily by the widespread adoption of the heavy moldboard plow, which could turn the dense clay soils of northern Europe far more effectively than the scratch plows previously in use. Evidence shows that population growth and the expansion of cultivated land both followed the spread of heavy plow use across the region.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historians' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The heavy moldboard plow was significantly more expensive to produce and maintain than the scratch plow, requiring collective farming arrangements to become economically viable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tenth through twelfth centuries in northern Europe did not experience any unusual improvement in climate or rainfall patterns relative to preceding centuries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medieval European monasteries played a significant role in disseminating knowledge of the heavy plow's advantages to surrounding farming communities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Population growth in medieval Europe was accompanied by the founding of numerous new towns and a measurable increase in long-distance trade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The scratch plow had been the dominant agricultural implement in northern Europe for more than five centuries before the heavy plow was introduced.

explanations.correct: The most powerful alternative explanation for increased agricultural productivity in this period would be a concurrent improvement in climate or rainfall. Ruling out any such climatic improvement leaves the heavy plow as the most plausible cause of the productivity gains, directly strengthening the historians' argument.
explanations.A: Interesting social history about plow economics, but this supports a neighboring claim about the organizational consequences of plow adoption rather than confirming that the plow caused the productivity increase. This is the 'strengthens a different conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Ruling out climatic improvement as an alternative explanation is the most direct way to support a causal attribution to the heavy plow.
explanations.C: Shows a mechanism by which knowledge of the plow spread—relevant to the rate of adoption but not to whether the plow, once adopted, caused the productivity gains. This is the 'accurate but irrelevant' trap.
explanations.D: Town founding and trade expansion are downstream effects of population growth, not causes of agricultural productivity—this does not address the causal chain at issue. This is the 'unwarranted comparison' trap.
explanations.E: Establishes the scratch plow's long dominance but says nothing about why the new plow caused the productivity increase rather than some other concurrent factor. Neutral at best.

difficultyReason: EXCEPT format. The argument concerns arts funding and audience engagement. Four answers each strengthen a step in the argument; the exception addresses a collateral benefit that does not bear on the argument's conclusion.
stimulus: Arts administrator: Publicly funded community arts programs consistently report higher audience attendance figures than privately funded programs of comparable size. Because public funding insulates programs from commercial pressures to stage only widely popular productions, publicly funded programs can take greater artistic risks. Greater artistic risk-taking attracts more engaged audiences. Therefore, the best way to grow arts audiences is to increase public funding for community arts programs.
questionStem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the arts administrator's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surveys of arts audiences show that attendees cite artistic originality and risk-taking as primary reasons for their continued engagement with community arts programs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Privately funded community arts programs that lose commercial sponsorship tend to reduce the variety of productions they stage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Community arts programs that increased their public funding allocation subsequently reported significant growth in first-time audience members.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Artists employed by publicly funded community programs report higher levels of job satisfaction and creative fulfillment than those employed by privately funded programs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In regions where public arts funding was reduced, community arts programs reported declining attendance within two years of the funding cuts.

explanations.correct: Artist job satisfaction and creative fulfillment are collateral benefits of public funding that do not bear on the argument's conclusion about audience growth. The argument is about audience engagement, not artist welfare. This choice does not strengthen any link in the chain from public funding to audience growth.
explanations.A: Strengthens—confirms the key premise that artistic risk-taking is what attracts and retains audiences.
explanations.B: Strengthens—confirms that private funding creates commercial pressure that limits artistic variety, supporting the mechanism behind public funding's advantage.
explanations.C: Strengthens—provides direct empirical support for the conclusion that increasing public funding grows arts audiences.
explanations.D: Correct (does not strengthen). Artist satisfaction is a separate benefit of public funding, not relevant to the audience-growth conclusion.
explanations.E: Strengthens—provides counterfactual evidence that reducing public funding reduces attendance, which by contrapositive supports the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument in environmental science requiring confirmation of a non-obvious mechanistic assumption. Trap choices include one that sounds like a strengthener but introduces an alternative causal path, and one that is only relevant to a collateral prediction.
stimulus: Environmental scientists predict that the reintroduction of gray wolves into a national forest ecosystem will lead to a measurable increase in riverbank vegetation density within a decade. Their reasoning: wolf predation pressure will cause elk herds to avoid grazing in riparian zones, allowing vegetation in those zones to recover. This is the same cascade of effects observed in Yellowstone National Park following wolf reintroduction there.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the scientists' prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The national forest's elk population currently grazes extensively in riparian zones and has been identified as the primary cause of riverbank vegetation loss in recent ecological assessments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gray wolves in Yellowstone National Park have expanded their territory significantly since reintroduction, colonizing areas well beyond the original release sites.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The national forest has a terrain and hydrology profile closely comparable to that of the Yellowstone ecosystem where the vegetation recovery was observed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several conservation organizations have endorsed the wolf reintroduction plan as consistent with best practices for apex predator restoration.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Riverbank vegetation density in other forests where wolves are absent has continued to decline at rates similar to the national forest's current rate of decline.

explanations.correct: The argument is analogical: the Yellowstone cascade of effects is assumed to apply to the national forest. Confirming that the national forest's terrain and hydrology are closely comparable to Yellowstone's closes the most critical gap in the analogy, making it much more likely that the same causal cascade will unfold.
explanations.A: Confirms that elk are currently responsible for vegetation loss—which supports the first step in the chain—but the argument already assumes elk grazing is the problem. This strengthens a premise already established rather than the non-obvious analogical link. Weaker than (C).
explanations.B: Describes wolf behavior in Yellowstone but does not address whether the reintroduction in the national forest will produce the same vegetation effects. This is the 'strengthens a different conclusion' trap (about wolves' range expansion, not vegetation recovery mechanisms).
explanations.C: Correct. Ecological comparability between the two sites is the load-bearing assumption of the analogy.
explanations.D: Endorsement by conservation organizations is an appeal to authority and does not address the mechanistic or analogical chain. This is the 'accurate but irrelevant' trap.
explanations.E: Shows that absent wolves, vegetation continues to decline—which is consistent with the argument but does not confirm that wolf reintroduction specifically will cause the recovery, because other factors might differ. Weaker than (C).

difficultyReason: Economic policy argument where the correct answer addresses an unstated but load-bearing assumption about price elasticity. Traps include a choice that strengthens a different part of the argument and a sophisticated disguised weakener.
stimulus: A government economist argues that imposing a tax on sugary beverages will reduce consumption of those beverages among low-income consumers. The economist points to data showing that low-income households currently spend a higher proportion of their income on sugary beverages than high-income households, indicating that low-income consumers are more sensitive to price changes in these products than high-income consumers.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In jurisdictions that have enacted sugary beverage taxes, low-income consumers reduced their purchases of taxed beverages by a greater percentage than high-income consumers did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-income households in the surveyed region spend more total dollars on sugary beverages than low-income households, despite the lower proportional spending.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proposed tax would be levied on manufacturers rather than directly on retail consumers, though manufacturers have historically passed such costs to consumers through price increases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public health studies have found that reduced consumption of sugary beverages is associated with lower rates of type 2 diabetes and obesity in population-level analyses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low-income consumers in the region have access to lower-cost unsweetened beverage alternatives, such as tap water and store-brand beverages, that could substitute for sugary beverages.

explanations.correct: The economist's argument requires that higher price sensitivity (as inferred from proportional spending) actually translates into behavioral changes when prices rise. Direct evidence from jurisdictions that enacted the tax—showing low-income consumers reduced purchases more than high-income consumers—confirms this chain from price sensitivity to reduced consumption, directly strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Real-world evidence that the tax produces the predicted differential effect on low-income consumers closes the gap between price sensitivity and behavioral response.
explanations.B: The total-dollar spending of high-income households is a distraction—it does not address whether low-income consumers will reduce consumption when a tax is imposed. This is the 'accurate but irrelevant' trap.
explanations.C: Confirms the tax will reach consumers as a price increase—which is a necessary condition for the argument to work—but is a weaker strengthener than (A) because it only establishes mechanism delivery, not the behavioral response. It also introduces the manufacturer intermediary as a mild complication.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different argument—about the health benefits of reduced consumption—rather than the economist's specific argument about whether the tax will cause reduced consumption among low-income consumers. This is the 'strengthens a different conclusion' trap.
explanations.E: Showing that substitutes exist is a necessary condition for price-sensitive consumers to actually reduce consumption (they need somewhere to switch). This is a meaningful strengthener but weaker than (A) because it only confirms substitutability exists rather than confirming that the tax actually caused the predicted behavioral shift.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy argument with a normative conclusion. The correct answer confirms a load-bearing empirical assumption underlying the normative inference. Traps include a choice that supports the normative principle in general but not the specific application, and a sophisticated disguised weakener.
stimulus: Bioethicist: Pharmaceutical companies should be required to publish the full results of all clinical trials they sponsor, including trials with negative or inconclusive outcomes. Currently, trials with positive outcomes are published at a far higher rate than trials with negative outcomes. This selective publication distorts the body of medical evidence available to prescribing physicians, who may therefore overestimate the efficacy of certain drugs when making treatment decisions.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the bioethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Physicians who were shown a complete set of trial results for a drug, including negative outcomes, revised their efficacy estimates for that drug significantly downward compared to physicians shown only the published positive results.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regulatory agencies in several countries require pharmaceutical companies to register clinical trials before they begin but do not require publication of results.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The principle that decision-makers should have access to complete and accurate information before making consequential choices is widely endorsed in professional codes of ethics.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some pharmaceutical companies voluntarily share unpublished trial data with regulators upon request, though this data is not made available to prescribing physicians.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Academic medical journals have begun implementing policies requiring disclosure of all trial phases as a condition of manuscript submission.

explanations.correct: The bioethicist's argument depends on the empirical claim that selective publication actually causes physicians to overestimate drug efficacy. Direct evidence that physicians given complete trial data—including negative results—significantly revised their efficacy estimates downward compared to physicians given only positive results confirms this causal mechanism and directly supports the conclusion that mandatory full publication would correct overestimation.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirms the core causal mechanism: selective publication causes overestimation, and access to full results corrects it.
explanations.B: Describes the current regulatory gap (registration without publication requirements)—this is consistent with the argument's premise but does not add new support to the conclusion about the effect of selective publication on physician decision-making. This is the 'accurate but irrelevant' trap.
explanations.C: Supports the general normative principle behind the argument but does not confirm the specific empirical mechanism—that selective publication actually distorts physician judgment in the way the bioethicist claims. This is the 'strengthens a different conclusion' trap (the general principle vs. this specific application).
explanations.D: Introduces a partial voluntary alternative to mandatory publication, noting that it still doesn't reach prescribing physicians. This is a mild strengthener (shows the current voluntary system is insufficient) but does not confirm the core mechanism. Weaker than (A).
explanations.E: Journal disclosure policies address one channel of the publication problem but do not confirm that selective publication actually causes physician overestimation—the key causal claim. This is the 'accurate but irrelevant' trap.
